title: UPSC Foundation Notes · Polity
description: Beginner-first bilingual notes with clear explanations, Prelims facts, Mains angles and active recall. Cross-check legal details against the latest official text.

chapters.subject: Indian Polity
chapters.title: Constitutionalism: Limited Government
chapters.summary: Constitutionalism ensures that public power remains limited by law, rights and accountability.

sections.heading: Meaning
body: A constitution establishes institutions and distributes powers. Constitutionalism adds the principle that government is not above the law.
A written constitution alone does not guarantee constitutionalism. Public power must be meaningfully constrained and accountable.

sections.heading: Core principles
bullets: Limited government: authorities have defined powers.
Rule of law: public decisions need legal authority and must follow fair procedures.
Fundamental rights: individuals have enforceable protections.
Checks and balances: institutions scrutinise and restrain misuse of power.
Independent judiciary: courts can review unconstitutional action.
Accountability: elections, legislatures, audits and transparency scrutinise government.

sections.heading: Indian context
body: India combines parliamentary government, judicial review, federalism, Fundamental Rights and an independent judiciary.
The basic structure doctrine limits Parliament's amending power: an amendment cannot destroy the Constitution's basic structure.

prelims: Constitutionalism is broader than merely possessing a written constitution.
Judicial review is one important check, not the only check.
The basic structure doctrine was articulated in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973).
mains: Explain how constitutionalism prevents arbitrary exercise of executive power.
Use judicial review, parliamentary accountability, federalism and rights protection as examples.
Balance institutional checks with effective governance.

recall.q: Does a written constitution automatically ensure constitutionalism?
recall.a: No. Effective limits on power, rule of law, rights and accountability are also necessary.

recall.q: Name two checks on government power in India.
recall.a: Judicial review and parliamentary accountability are two examples.

chapters.tamil: அரசாங்கத்துக்கு அதிகாரம் இருப்பது மட்டும் போதாது. அந்த அதிகாரம் சட்டம், உரிமைகள் மற்றும் பொறுப்புணர்வு மூலம் கட்டுப்படுத்தப்பட வேண்டும் என்பதே Constitutionalism.

chapters.subject: Indian Polity
chapters.title: The Preamble: Constitutional Vision
chapters.summary: The Preamble introduces the source of constitutional authority, nature of the Indian state and goals for citizens.

sections.heading: What it expresses
bullets: Authority: the Constitution derives its authority from the people of India.
Nature of the state: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic.
Objectives: Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity.
It highlights individual dignity and the unity and integrity of the Nation.

sections.heading: Legal position
body: The Preamble is part of the Constitution, as held in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).
It is not an independent source of legislative power and is not directly enforceable by itself.
It helps courts interpret constitutional provisions where meaning is uncertain.

sections.heading: Amendment
body: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 added the words Socialist, Secular and Integrity.

prelims: The Preamble has been amended once, by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.
It is part of the Constitution but is not independently enforceable.
Republic means the head of state is not a hereditary monarch.
mains: Connect Preamble ideals with rights, welfare policy, secular governance and social justice.
Discuss the gap between constitutional ideals and lived outcomes, with institutional remedies.

recall.q: Which amendment added Socialist, Secular and Integrity?
Does the Preamble independently confer legislative power?
recall.a: No. It guides interpretation but is not an independent source of power.

chapters.tamil: முன்னுரை அரசியலமைப்பின் நோக்கத்தையும் இந்தியா எந்த வகையான நாடாக இருக்க வேண்டும் என்பதையும் சுருக்கமாகக் கூறுகிறது.

chapters.subject: Indian Polity
chapters.title: Fundamental Rights: Protection and Limits
chapters.summary: Fundamental Rights protect liberty and equality while allowing constitutionally defined restrictions and remedies.

sections.heading: Constitutional location
body: Part III (Articles 12–35) contains Fundamental Rights.
Article 32 allows a person to approach the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. High Courts issue writs under Article 226, whose scope is wider.

sections.heading: Six broad categories
bullets: Right to Equality (Articles 14–18).
Right to Freedom (Articles 19–22).
Right against Exploitation (Articles 23–24).
Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25–28).
Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29–30).
Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32).

sections.heading: Important distinctions
body: Article 14 guarantees equality before law and equal protection of laws; it does not require identical treatment in every situation.
Article 19 freedoms are available to citizens and are subject to constitutionally specified reasonable restrictions.
Article 21 protects life and personal liberty and has received broad judicial interpretation.
The Right to Property is a constitutional legal right under Article 300A, not a Fundamental Right.

prelims: Article 32: Supreme Court remedy; Article 226: High Court writ jurisdiction.
mains: Discuss how rights protect dignity while permitting reasonable regulation for public purposes.
Use proportionality, access to justice and vulnerable-group perspectives where relevant.

recall.q: Is the Right to Property a Fundamental Right today?
recall.a: No. It is a constitutional legal right under Article 300A.

recall.q: Which Article provides the right to approach the Supreme Court to enforce Fundamental Rights?

chapters.tamil: அடிப்படை உரிமைகள் சுதந்திரம், சமத்துவம் மற்றும் மனித கண்ணியத்தைப் பாதுகாக்கின்றன. சில உரிமைகளுக்கு அரசியலமைப்பு அனுமதிக்கும் நியாயமான கட்டுப்பாடுகள் இருக்கலாம்.

chapters.subject: Indian Polity
chapters.title: Directive Principles of State Policy
chapters.summary: DPSPs guide the State towards a just social and economic order; they are not directly enforceable by courts.

sections.heading: Constitutional position
body: Directive Principles are in Part IV, Articles 36–51.
Article 37 says they are not enforceable by any court, but are fundamental in governance and it is the duty of the State to apply them in making laws.

sections.heading: Broad themes
bullets: Social and economic justice: reduce inequalities and promote welfare.
Gandhian orientation: village panchayats and weaker sections.
Liberal-intellectual principles: environment, judiciary-executive separation and international peace.
These are study classifications; the Constitution does not formally label every article this way.

sections.heading: Relationship with Fundamental Rights
body: Fundamental Rights and DPSPs are intended to complement each other.
The Supreme Court has emphasised harmony and balance between Parts III and IV.

prelims: Article 37: non-justiciable but fundamental in governance.
Article 40 concerns village panchayats; Article 48A concerns environment and forests.
mains: Explain how DPSPs shape welfare legislation and public policy.
Discuss implementation, fiscal capacity and measurable outcomes.

recall.q: Are DPSPs directly enforceable by courts?
recall.a: No. Article 37 makes them non-justiciable but fundamental in governance.

chapters.tamil: அரசு மக்கள் நலன், சமூக நீதி மற்றும் சமத்துவத்தை மேம்படுத்த வழிகாட்டும் கொள்கைகளே DPSP. நீதிமன்றத்தில் நேரடியாக அமல்படுத்த முடியாது; ஆனால் ஆட்சியில் அவை முக்கியமானவை.

chapters.subject: Indian Polity
chapters.title: Parliament: Law-making and Accountability
chapters.summary: Parliament makes laws, controls public finance, represents citizens and holds the executive accountable.

sections.heading: Constitutional structure
body: Under Article 79, Parliament consists of the President and two Houses: Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha.
The President is part of Parliament but is not a member of either House.

sections.heading: Core functions
bullets: Legislative: debates and passes laws within Parliament's competence.
Financial: scrutinises taxation, expenditure and the Union Budget.
Executive accountability: questions, debates, motions and committees examine government action.
Representative and deliberative: brings public and regional concerns into national decision-making.
Constitutional: exercises amendment power under Article 368, subject to basic structure limits.

sections.heading: Why committees matter
body: Parliamentary committees examine bills, budgets and policy details in smaller forums.
Committee scrutiny can improve technical review, deliberation and executive oversight.

prelims: Money Bills are governed by Article 110; the Speaker certifies whether a Bill is a Money Bill.
Rajya Sabha is a permanent House; one-third of members retire every second year.
mains: Assess Parliament's role in executive accountability and quality law-making.
Discuss disruptions, limited scrutiny and committee referrals with balanced reforms.

recall.q: Who forms part of Parliament under Article 79?
recall.a: The President, Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha.
No. It is a permanent House; one-third of members retire every second year.

chapters.tamil: நாடாளுமன்றம் சட்டம் இயற்றுவது மட்டுமல்ல; அரசின் செலவுகள், கொள்கைகள் மற்றும் நிர்வாகத்தையும் கண்காணிக்கிறது.

chapters.subject: Indian Polity
chapters.title: Indian Federalism: Union and States
chapters.summary: India combines constitutional division of powers with institutions and practices that require Union–State cooperation.

sections.heading: Distribution of powers
body: Part XI and the Seventh Schedule distribute legislative subjects across Union, State and Concurrent Lists.
Parliament has residuary legislative power under Article 248.
In the Concurrent List, both Parliament and State Legislatures can legislate; Article 254 addresses repugnancy subject to constitutional conditions.

sections.heading: Indian features
bullets: Written and supreme Constitution.
Constitutional division of legislative and executive powers.
Independent judiciary to interpret the division of powers.
A comparatively strong Union in specified circumstances.
Single citizenship and an integrated judicial system.

sections.heading: Cooperative and competitive federalism
body: Cooperative federalism involves joint problem-solving through consultation.
Competitive federalism encourages States to improve performance and public-service delivery.
Inter-State Council (Article 263), Finance Commission (Article 280) and GST Council (Article 279A) are important institutions.

prelims: Seventh Schedule: Union, State and Concurrent Lists.
Article 263: Inter-State Council; Article 280: Finance Commission; Article 279A: GST Council.
Residuary legislative powers are vested in Parliament.
mains: Examine how fiscal arrangements and centrally sponsored schemes shape Union–State relations.
Suggest predictable consultation, transparent transfers and stronger inter-governmental forums.

recall.q: Which Schedule contains the three legislative lists?
Which Article provides for the GST Council?

chapters.tamil: மத்திய அரசு மற்றும் மாநில அரசுகளுக்கு இடையே அதிகாரங்கள் அரசியலமைப்பால் பகிரப்பட்டுள்ளன. நாட்டின் வளர்ச்சிக்கு இரு நிலை அரசுகளும் இணைந்து செயல்படுவது முக்கியம்.
